prompt: What are the common mistakes with dependency injection in C# and how can they be avoided?
completion:
### Dependency Injection in C# – The Most Common Pitfalls & How to Dodge Them Dependency Injection (DI) is a design pattern that swaps “who does the work” for “who supplies the work”. In .NET Core (and its descendants) the built‑in `IServiceCollection`/`IServiceProvider` combo is the most common DI container. It’s powerful, but if you abuse it you’ll quickly find yourself with brittle code, hidden bugs, and hard‑to‑test classes. Below is a **shopping list of the most frequent mistakes** you’ll see in real projects, why they’re bad, and concrete ways to avoid them (or fix them later). The patterns and code snippets are aimed at the *ASP.NET Core / .NET 6+* world, but the ideas translate to any C# DI container. | # | Common Mistake | Why It’s Bad | How to Avoid / Fix | |---|----------------|--------------|--------------------| | 1 | **Injecting `IServiceProvider` (the “Service Locator” anti‑pattern)** | The class hides its true dependencies and becomes impossible to test in isolation. | **Never** inject `IServiceProvider`. If you need a factory for a family of objects, expose an *interface* for the factory (`IProductFactory`) or use `IOptionsMonitor`, `IEnumerable`, `Func`, or `Lazy` where appropriate. | | 2 | **Registering services with the wrong lifetime** | A `Singleton` that captures a `Scoped` service will either keep a stale instance (leading to stale state) or keep a `Scoped` object alive longer than a request (memory leak). | • Use **Transient** for short‑lived, stateless services.
• Use **Scoped** for per‑request or per‑unit‑of‑work objects (DbContext, UnitOfWork).
• Use **Singleton** only for truly immutable, thread‑safe objects (configuration, logging).
• If a Singleton needs a Scoped dependency, inject a `Func` or a factory that creates the Scoped object per call. | | 3 | **Injecting too many dependencies into one constructor** | A constructor with 5+ parameters usually indicates the class violates SRP (Single Responsibility Principle). | • Refactor: split responsibilities, introduce a *facade* or *aggregate service* that hides the sub‑services.
• If you only need a handful of methods from a large service, consider a lightweight interface or a **DTO** to reduce coupling. | | 4 | **Injecting concrete classes instead of abstractions** | Tight coupling makes swapping implementations (e.g., mocking a repository) impossible. | • Register an interface (`IUserRepository`) and inject that.
• Only expose *abstract* contracts to the consuming class. | | 5 | **Circular dependencies** | Two services depend on each other → constructor injection fails with `InvalidOperationException`. | • Break the cycle: use a **factory** or **Mediator** pattern.
• Use `Lazy` or `IServiceProvider.GetService()` inside the constructor body (but avoid this if you can).
• Re‑evaluate design – maybe a new domain concept (e.g., a “CommandHandler” that orchestrates both). | | 6 | **Injecting a container‑specific type into domain logic** (e.g., `IHttpContextAccessor` in a domain service) | Domain services should be container‑agnostic. | • Move container‑specific code to an *application layer* or *infrastructure layer*.
• Use **Adapter** or **Strategy** pattern to translate from `HttpContext` to a plain DTO. | | 7 | **Registering services in the wrong part of the app** (e.g., forgetting to register a service in `Program.cs`) | Runtime errors (`InvalidOperationException: No service for type … was registered.`) | • Keep **one composition root** (usually `Program.cs` / `Startup.cs`).
• Create extension methods like `services.AddMyDomain()` to group registrations. | | 8 | **Using property injection instead of constructor injection** | Property injection can leave the object in an inconsistent state (properties may remain null). | • Prefer constructor injection.
• Use property injection only when you absolutely must (e.g., for optional dependencies or for libraries that don’t support constructor injection). | | 9 | **Injecting static or singleton helpers (e.g., `new LoggerFactory()`)** | You lose the benefits of DI and break testability. | • Register `ILoggerFactory` as a singleton via `services.AddLogging()`.
• Inject `ILogger` into classes; the DI container will supply the correct logger. | |10 | **Injecting `DbContext` into a service that lives longer than a request** | `DbContext` is a scoped type; a long‑lived service holding onto it will cause stale data and EF Core exceptions. | • Keep the service itself *scoped*, or use a factory that creates a new `DbContext` per operation. | |11 | **Using the container to create objects manually** (`var foo = serviceProvider.GetService();`) | This breaks the inversion of control contract and mixes object creation with business logic. | • Let the container wire up everything; only use `GetService` in the composition root or in a *factory* that the container itself supplies. | |12 | **Forgetting to dispose disposable services** | Scoped services that implement `IDisposable` (e.g., `DbContext`) are disposed automatically, but if you resolve them manually you must call `Dispose()`. | • Don’t resolve manually.
• If you must, wrap in `using` or use `IAsyncDisposable` with `await using`. | |13 | **Registering open generics incorrectly** (e.g., `services.AddTransient(typeof(IRepository<>), typeof(Repository<>));` but forgetting to register a concrete generic parameter) | You get runtime errors when the container can’t construct a concrete closed generic type. | • Register the open generic once and let the container resolve closed types.
• Avoid overloading generic services unless necessary. | |14 | **Using DI for pure value objects or simple DTOs** | DI is meant for services, not for plain data holders. | • Don’t inject DTOs. Use them as constructor parameters or method arguments directly. | |15 | **Over‑abstraction** – creating an interface for every class | Increases surface area with little benefit and complicates registration. | • Apply the *Interface Segregation Principle*: only expose interfaces that clients actually depend on.
• Use interfaces where you need polymorphism or mocking; otherwise keep the concrete class. | --- ## Practical “How‑to” Checklist | Step | What to do | Why it matters | |------|------------|----------------| | **1. Use constructor injection everywhere** | Guarantees that all dependencies are supplied at object creation. | The object is always fully initialized and immutable after construction. | | **2. Keep the constructor short** | Aim for 0–3 parameters; otherwise refactor. | Short constructors reflect SRP and easier to test. | | **3. Prefer abstractions** | Register an interface, inject the interface. | Enables swapping implementations (mocking, production vs test). | | **4. Match lifetimes** | Singleton → Singleton, Scoped → Scoped, Transient → Transient. | Avoid memory leaks and stale data. | | **5. Avoid service locator** | No `IServiceProvider` inside domain classes. | Keeps dependencies explicit and testable. | | **6. Handle circular dependencies** | Refactor, use factories, or Mediator. | Eliminates constructor recursion and `InvalidOperationException`. | | **7. Keep the composition root** | All registrations in `Program.cs` (or `Startup.cs`). | One place to see all wiring; easier to audit. | | **8. Use `IOptions` for configuration** | `services.Configure(Configuration.GetSection("MySettings"));` | Strongly‑typed config, change‑tracking, and validation. | | **9. Use `Lazy` or `Func` for expensive services** | `services.AddTransient(); services.AddTransient>(sp => new Lazy(() => sp.GetRequiredService()));` | Avoids constructing services you may not need. | | **10. Test with mocks** | `var mockRepo = new Mock(); mockRepo.Setup(r => r.Get(1)).Returns(new User());` | DI + mocks keep tests fast and isolated. | --- ## Sample “Right” vs “Wrong” Code **Wrong (Service Locator)** ```csharp public class UserService { private readonly IServiceProvider _provider; public UserService(IServiceProvider provider) => _provider = provider; public void Delete(int id) { var repo = _provider.GetRequiredService(); repo.Delete(id); } } ``` **Right (Constructor Injection)** ```csharp public interface IUserService { void Delete(int id); } public class UserService : IUserService { private readonly IUserRepository _repo; public UserService(IUserRepository repo) => _repo = repo; public void Delete(int id) => _repo.Delete(id); } ``` --- ## When to *Not* Use DI | Situation | Recommendation | |-----------|----------------| | **Pure static utility methods** | Keep them static; DI isn’t needed. | | **Small value objects** | Don’t register them; just instantiate. | | **One‑off “command” objects** | If they only wrap data for a single method, don’t inject them. | | **Legacy code that can’t be refactored** | Inject only what’s necessary; leave the rest as is. | --- ## Final Takeaway DI is a **tool** to make your code more modular, testable, and maintainable. Misusing it turns that tool into a *bottleneck*: * **Too many constructor parameters** → SRP violation. * **Wrong lifetime** → memory leaks or stale state. * **Service locator** → hidden dependencies, hard tests. * **Circular dependencies** → runtime errors. By following the checklist above, keeping your composition root tidy, and treating DI as a *contract* rather than a *magical magic* bean‑factory, you’ll avoid the most common pitfalls and keep your C# applications clean, robust, and easy to evolve. Happy injecting!
